extracted.intended_audience: publishers, printers, newspaper and pamphlet editors, and legal practitioners advising on periodical/press copyright and statutory regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and statutory requirements governing reviews, magazines, newspapers, and pamphlets: what may be copied or published, registration/affidavit/delivery obligations, content prohibitions, and penalties. Focuses on British press and stamp-duty statutes and case law treated in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of additions to an old work
rubrics_metrics.description: An action lies to recover damages for pirating the additions to an old work; injunctions are granted to prevent infringement of the copyright in the additional pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when Gray's poems were republished by Mason with many additional pieces, an injunction was immediately granted to prevent infringement of copyright in the additional pieces. The owner of new material added to an existing work has enforceable rights against pirates of those additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions restraining printing of notes/embellishments
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be granted to restrain anyone from printing the notes published with a new edition of an old book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a person was enjoined from printing Paradise Lost with Dr. Newton's notes even though Paradise Lost itself could be republished; mixing a small number of new notes with old ones to conceal piracy is colourable and will not prevent relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes/embellishments do not confer right to print original
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes or embellishments to a book (the copyright of which is not expired) confer no power to print the original book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors adding notes cannot claim a right to print the underlying copyrighted text; statutes granting printing rights (e.g., king's/printer's patent) may not be overridden by collusive notes to gain wider printing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright in critic's corrections and alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic has copyright even in the verbal corrections and alterations which he makes to a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: critics' published corrections (e.g., Dr. Bentley's) are protectable as original additions/alterations and are enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original essays in reviews are treated as separate works
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays or original pieces published in reviews or magazines are to be viewed in the same light as though published by themselves, whether composed by the proprietor or procured for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original contributions in periodicals enjoy copyright protection independently of the periodical as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity limitation on extracts in reviews (quotations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extracts must not be made too freely: sufficient may be taken to form a correct idea of the whole, but no one may publish either the whole or principal part of another's composition under the pretence of quoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A review must not serve as a substitute for the book reviewed; if so much is extracted that it communicates the same knowledge as the original, it is actionable. The intention to pirate can usually be inferred from the quantity copied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and limits of critical remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks made by a critic must not be personal or impugn the moral character of the author; criticisms on the merits of the work, without reference to the individual, may be justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair and candid criticism—even harsh or ridiculing—on the work itself is permissible; introducing personal attacks or fabrications risks liability (e.g., libel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abridgments and translations treated like other abridgments/translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Abridgments and translations published in reviews are judged in the same manner as abridgments and translations in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard rules on originality, quotation limits, and infringement apply to abridgments/translations appearing in periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and physical-size limits of a newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper is defined as containing public news, intelligence, or occurrences printed in Great Britain to be dispersed publicly, and may consist of a sheet, half sheet, or other piece of paper; it must not exceed thirty-two inches in length and twenty-two inches in breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory size limits (cited acts) are part of the legal definition and relevant to classification and stamp-duty treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit and registration before publishing a newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit must be delivered into the Stamp Office before a newspaper is published (penalty £100). The affidavit must be renewed upon every change of circumstances and must make known the names and residences of the printer and publishers and specify proprietors as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are no more than two proprietors they must be specified; if more than two, the two who possess shares not less in value than the others must be named. The affidavit must include a description of the printing house and the paper's title. Misrepresentation or omission can lead to perjury penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit evidentiary effect and penalties for false certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: The affidavit filed (or a certified copy signed by commissioners) is evidence of itself; a false certificate or affidavit renders its maker liable to penalties (e.g., £100).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors need not prove purchase of the newspaper; certified copies obtained from commissioners are admissible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names on the newspaper and delivery of copy to commissioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of the printers and publishers must appear on the newspaper itself; a copy signed by the printer or publisher must be delivered within six days to the commissioners of stamps under a penalty of £100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sample may be produced within two years at the applicant's expense as evidence in court. A printer whose name does not appear cannot recover in an action for printing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on publishers/hawkers distributing newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: No hawker of newspapers or other persons is allowed to let out any newspaper from house to house (or to different persons) on pain of forfeiting 5s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory restriction on modes of distribution intended to control circulation and stamp-duty compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of blasphemous, seditious, or libellous content
rubrics_metrics.description: In neither essays nor observations can anything blasphemous, seditious, or libellous be published; the proprietor is answerable, criminally and civilly, for the acts of his agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The whole publication is legally considered written by the proprietor. When the act is unlawful (e.g., libel on the King), the proof of justification lies on the defendant; failure to justify implies criminal intent on proprietor even if he did not author the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conducting a newspaper to advantage enemies or sending to enemy countries
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper must not be conducted for the advantage of the enemies of the country; sending a newspaper to a foreign country not at amity with England is penalized (e.g., £00) and suspected persons may be taken before a justice and forfeit large sums for non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory penalties and investigatory powers attach to transmissions to hostile jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of reports of courts and parliament — truth and court discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct statements of what passes in a court of justice may be published unless the Court indicates it should not be published yet; in actions for libel, it must be proved that the newspaper's account contains in substance precisely what was delivered by the Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing personal observations with court reports or publishing material that prejudices parties can be actionable; reports must be true copies and, where necessary, publication may be restrained to avoid prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for advertisements and limits on relying on third-party ads
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor cannot, in answer to an indictment, assert that the objectionable part was an advertisement of another person and therefore avoid accountability; some advertisements reflecting on individuals may still be inserted if made in good faith and for a legitimate purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain advertisements are statutorily prohibited (e.g., offices for illegal insurances, lottery proposals) with specified penalties. Advertising a public debate on the Lord's day carries penalties and time limits for actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory prohibitions on certain advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes impose penalties (e.g., £100 or £50) for advertising illegal insurance schemes, lottery-related proposals, rewards promising no questions, or public debates on the Lord's day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers risk direct statutory penalties for carrying prohibited advertisements; distributors (e.g., hand-bill distributors) may also be criminally liable under the lottery acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper as legal evidence and the London Gazette's special status
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute, a common newspaper is legal evidence for particular purposes (e.g., notices of meetings, private-bill motions), and notices published in the London Gazette are deemed good and sufficient notice to all his majesty's subjects for many statutory purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Gazette's publication is treated as authoritative for statutory notices like partnership dissolutions, proclamations for felons, and bank-related notices; reliance on Gazette notice may or may not substitute for individual notice depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and classification of pamphlets by sheet count and size
rubrics_metrics.description: A pamphlet is a book consisting of one sheet and not exceeding eight sheets in octavo, or not exceeding twelve sheets in quarto, or twenty sheets in folio. Pamphlets are distinguished into larger (more than two sheets) and smaller (two sheets or less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification affects stamp-duty, manner of publication, and whether they are treated like books or assimilated to newspapers (especially smaller political pamphlets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller political pamphlets assimilated to newspapers (statutory test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller political pamphlets are described by statute (60 Geo. III c. 9) as pamphlets/papers containing public news, intelligence, occurrences, or remarks thereon, printed for sale and published periodically or in parts at intervals not exceeding twenty-six days, where any issue does not exceed two sheets and is of specified minimum dimensions, or sold for less than sixpence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such pamphlets are to be deemed within the newspaper statutes and thereby subject to the same regulatory/stamp-duty and penal rules as newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizance/bond requirement for publishing smaller political pamphlets (post-1819)
rubrics_metrics.description: No person, after thirty days from 5 Dec. 1819, may publish a newspaper or such smaller pamphlets unless he has entered into a recognizance before a Baron of the Exchequer or executed a bond to the King with sureties (amounts differing by location), conditioned for payment of penalties for publishing blasphemous or seditious libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical amounts: three hundred pounds with sureties for London (within 20 miles) and two hundred pounds if printed elsewhere; failure to renew or replace sureties (e.g., if a surety paid penalty or becomes bankrupt) bars publication until new recognizance/bond is entered. A surety may withdraw with 20 days' notice; lists of recognizances are sent quarterly and bonds transmitted by the justice within ten days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of pamphlet copies to commissioners of stamps
rubrics_metrics.description: A pamphlet must be delivered on its day of publication (or within six days) to the commissioners of stamps signed by the printer or publisher with his name and place of abode, under a penalty of £100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commissioners refuse to receive or pay for a copy because they believe it not within the act, they must, if required, deliver a certificate that a copy was duly offered, which exempts the printer/publisher from penalties.
